bbc_card_1.headline: German Chancellor Merz calls state election a 'disaster' for his party but vows to stay on
bbc_card_1.description: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
bbc_card_1.article_content:
Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.

In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the far-right AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party.

In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).

Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.

Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms.

"The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward".

"I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.

As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration.

This is a party that knows it's in trouble, and its leader quickly went on the offensive, declaring that he is going nowhere.

Merz has long coveted the top job in German politics, and likely won't give it up easily.

Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected later on Sunday night, or even Monday morning.

Public broadcasters ZDF and ARD put the AfD ahead in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The party was projected to take 38% of the vote share in the state, according to ZDF, followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%.

However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it.

For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.

Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.

Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only been chancellor for 16 months.

On Sunday, Burkard Dregger, a CDU member of the Senate in Berlin, told the BBC it was right that Merz should stay on. "He has a lot of work to do and we don't have time to waste to form new government in the federal level".

He described the electorate as "impatient", adding that it was "not realistic to expect that every issue has been solved within one year.

"He has got four years and we have to give him the four years," Dregger said.

While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular.

The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support, while also alienating people further to the left.

bbc_card_2.headline: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
bbc_card_2.description: Princess Diana's brother describes press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and says he saw his sister cry "tears of despair" over interest in her.
bbc_card_2.article_content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's treatment at the hands of the media has "echoes" of what happened to his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.

He described press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and said it would be "beholden on people to learn from Diana's example".

The Sussexes, who recently returned to the UK from California six years after stepping back from royal duties, have been repeatedly critical of the media.

It comes after the BBC reported on Friday how Earl Spencer says he was "telling the truth" when he claimed King Charles said people would forget Diana "soon enough" in a phone call in the days after her death.

Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face.

"If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied.

"And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example.

"I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."

He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".

Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan.

He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."

Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997.

In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness".

His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK.

They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK.

Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear".

Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me".

In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m.

In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology.

Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly worded response to his claims about King Charles.

That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Earl Spencer accused the King of psychological manipulation over the palace's statement.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the King," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said".

Journalist Richard Kay, who had been close friends with Diana, also wrote in the newspaper on Sunday that in the week between her death and funeral, Earl Spencer had told him of a "furious row" with Charles.

"It was 'about the boys', but he was reluctant to go further," said Kay, adding that Earl Spencer said the then prince had been "utterly pathetic".

However, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House on Sunday, Dame Julia Cleverdon, a trusted aide and friend of the King, said the claims about his response to Diana's death did not reflect "the language or the behaviours of a man I've known for 40 years".

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

Dame Julia said: "To say that the Prince of Wales was elated and somehow took any pleasure... he was as if a 10-tonne truck had fallen on him.

Her own husband had died a fortnight before Diana and she said Charles "could not have been more supportive, loving, concerned about the children and interested".

bbc_card_4.headline: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipers
bbc_card_4.description: Trump said the updated plans were at the request of the US military and for national security purposes.
bbc_card_4.article_content:
US President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.

In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".

The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.

He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are.

Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month.

A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.

At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.

The Department of Defence declined to provide additional details when reached for comment.

Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.

card_2.headline: Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?
card_2.description: Germany needs more affordable homes, and it's willing to rewrite some rules to build them.
card_2.article_content:
Germany is confronting a growing housing crisis, as demand for homes in major cities continues to outpace supply.

Faced with rising rents, construction delays, and a shortage of affordable housing, policymakers, developers and urban planners are reconsidering long-standing building regulations and planning rules.

Measures once seen as politically or socially unacceptable are now part of the debate, as authorities seek ways to boost construction and cut costs.

The challenge is whether these reforms can deliver enough homes to ease pressure on the housing market.

card_3.headline: Record Ukrainian attack leaves Moscow ablaze on election day
card_3.description: 1,600 drones were fired at Moscow on the final day of Russian elections.
card_3.article_content:
Ukraine launched what Russian authorities described as the largest drone attack of the war against Moscow and its surrounding region, striking critical infrastructure including the Russian capital's largest oil refinery on the final day of parliamentary elections. The attack highlights Kyiv's continuing strategy of targeting Russia's energy sector while bringing the war deeper into Russian territory.

Russia analyst Jenny Mathers of Aberystwyth University told DW attacks on Moscow have significance far beyond their immediate military impact. "Strikes in Moscow city and Moscow region at any time are a major symbol of Ukrainian military expertise and military might," Mathers said. "On an election day, it's an additional signal that the Ukrainians are sending to the Russians."

card_4.headline: Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?
card_4.description: Middle East analyst Giorgio Cafiero: Saudi Arabia will have to make concessions to the Houthis to guarantee stability.
card_4.article_content:
Yemen's Houthi rebels have launched a ballistic missile toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, just days after the United States signaled it would not join any Saudi-led military campaign against the group.

Following Washington's decision, Riyadh has sought to deepen security cooperation with countries including the United Kingdom, France, Pakistan, and Egypt. But Middle East analyst Giorgio Cafiero tells DW's David Levitz that he thinks Saudi Arabia will ultimately have to make concessions to the Houthis to guarantee stability.

card_5.headline: Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist
card_5.description: He was early to back Facebook, early to back Donald Trump, and became a billionaire. But what drives Peter Thiel?
card_5.article_content:
He may not hog the limelight in the same way as Donald Trump, Elon Musk, or many of his other friends and associates, but Peter Thiel has a fair claim to be one of the world's most influential figures — as well as one of its richest.

Born in 1967 in Frankfurt am Main in what was then West Germany, the Thiel family moved to the US when Peter was just a year old. The family also spent six years in South-African occupied Namibia from 1971 to 1977.

Thiel's later rise to prominence came on the back of his tech firms and investments. His first major success was Paypal, a digital payments provider with which Musk was initially involved. Thiel then became the first outside investor in Facebook.

Today he also owns part of Musk's SpaceX, as well as OpenAI, and multiple other companies. Forbes puts his personal wealth at $35.7 billion (€31.1 billion).

But perhaps his most noteworthy company is Palantir. The surveillance, AI, and data-analytics company has won government contracts worth billions to create software for the Pentagon as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The company released a 22-point manifesto in April that critics said bore the imprint of "techno-fascism."

But Thiel could be considered as influential in politics as he is in business, and not just in the US.

Though several European countries, including the UK, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Spain are starting to reevaluate or end their governmental and military links with Palantir due to security concerns, the company is deeply embedded in security systems across the globe.

Thiel himself has recently moved to Argentina, where he has reportedly held talks with the country's right-wing president, Javier Milei, as the government proposes a series of regulations that include incentives for foreign companies and targets investments in AI data centers.

Thiel was an early backer, and later advisor, of Donald Trump, donating $1.25 million to Trump's 2016 election campaign and speaking at the Republican National Convention in the same year, at a time when Silicon Valley was broadly considered to be Democrat-leaning. Bar a hiatus between 2023 and 2025, he has been a generous donor to Republican campaigns and figures, including Vice President JD Vance.

Thiel's own political beliefs are not easy to pin down. He's been described as a libertarian nationalist and consistently expressed the belief that "technology is the alternative to politics."

He also shows a distrust of authorities, regulation, and liberal elites. This is partly born of a frustration with what Thiel considers inefficient decision-making by elected officials and voters.

"It's bordering on fascism," Max Chafkin, who wrote a 2021 biography of Thiel, told Time magazine. "He talks about how companies are better run than governments because they have a single decision-maker — a dictator, basically. He is hostile to the idea of democracy. That's pretty scary when you consider the role the companies that he's been involved in play."

These beliefs seemed to start to rise to the surface during his time at Stanford University in California. Thiel railed against the prevailing liberal campus ideology and founded the Stanford Review, a publication to express those contrary beliefs, something that would echo his current disdain for beliefs labeled as "woke."

Thiel was raised in a strongly Christian household, and there is little doubt that his religion has colored his life and career. Thiel recently described himself as a "small 'o' orthodox Christian," something which seems to influence his conservative politics. His homosexuality, and marriage to American financier Matt Danzeisen, seem to many go against that grain. But paradox is not unusual for Thiel.

More recently, he has become preoccupied with the concept of the antichrist, touring with a series of lectures all over the world during the last few years. Rather than the figure depicted in the Bible, Thiel sees this as someone, or some group, who will deliver the apocalypse "by playing on our fears of technology and seducing us into decadence with the antichrist's slogan: Peace and safety."

Among those who have been, somewhat vaguely, cast in the role of soldiers of the antichrist have been environmental activist Greta Thunberg, whom he sees as a "Luddite who wants to stop all science," or governments that seek to regulate AI. He accused Pope Leo XIV of "working for the Chinese communists" in July after the pontiff warned about the "risk of dehumanization" by AI.

Despite his deep association with tech, Thiel also benefits from his relationships with powerful people, Musk, Trump, and Vance among them.

"I've built some great friendships over the years with people I've worked with," Thiel told the Washington Post in 2014. "And I think that's a really important part of what enables one to be successful in the long run in our society."

Many observers think that Thiel may be using his relationship with Vance to help protect himself and his business interests in the future, with the vice presidentconsidered the most likely Republican to succeed Trump.

The pair met back in 2011 when Thiel gave a talk at Yale Law School. Vance, whose religious beliefs and politics have since shifted, wrote in Christian magazine The Lamp that Thiel "defied the social template I had constructed — that dumb people were Christians and smart ones atheists."

Thiel then reportedly became a mentor figure for Vance, before smoothing the relationship between Vance and Trump as Vance U-turned from previous opposition to the president to join his 2024 ticket. Most notably though, Thiel donated $15 million to Vance's Senate campaign in 2022, the largest amount ever donated to a single US Senate candidate.

The recent calls to slow the pace of AI, made in part by CEOs in similar positions to Thiel, may end up having an impact on Thiel's business interests. But his distinct character and connections have so far kept him a step ahead.

Edited by Carla Bleiker

card_6.headline: Flushed away: The fertilizer hidden in human pee and poop
card_6.description: Scientists are turning pee, poop and sewage into fertilizers. Could this help close the nutrient loop?
card_6.article_content:
Every year, huge amounts of valuable nutrients are flushed down our toilets. Yet farmers depend on many of those same nutrients, including nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, to grow food.

At the same time, Europe continues to rely heavily on mineral fertilizers, even as fertilizer prices have risen sharply in recent years.

So why do we go to such lengths to produce and mine nutrients for food, only to flush some of them away afterward?

Around the world, researchers are developing technologies to turn human waste into fertilizer.

In Sweden, researchers have developed toilets that separate urine from other waste at the source. The collected urine can then be stabilized and dried into a concentrated fertilizer product that is easier for farmers to transport and use.

Similar ideas are being tested elsewhere.

Human feces can also be turned into fertilizer. On an organic farm in Mexico, feces from dry toilets is mixed with materials such as straw and composted for several months. High temperatures during composting help destroy pathogens, leaving behind a soil-like fertilizer that can be used to grow vegetables.

At Germany's Emscher Mündung wastewater treatment plant, the SUSKULT project is testing how nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium can be recovered from wastewater and turned into liquid fertilizer.

Around 1,000 liters (some 260 gallons) of wastewater flow through the plant every second. Researchers estimate that recovering just 10% of its nutrient potential could provide enough nutrients to grow around 3% of the tomatoes Germany consumes in a year.

Together, these projects show how human waste could help recycle valuable resources and support a more circular food system.

card_8.headline: Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
card_8.article_content:
This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Saturday, September 19 and Sunday, September 20:

India thrashed Bangladesh by 114 runs in the Asian Games women's cricket semi-final on Sunday, with opener Shafali Verma striking a maiden century and Smriti Mandhana becoming the all-time leading run-scorer in women's T20 internationals.

Verma finished unbeaten on 100 off 49 balls, reaching triple figures off the final delivery of India's innings. It marked the first century in the history of Asian Games women's cricket, Indian wire service ANI reported, making Verma just the third Indian woman to score a T20I hundred, joining Mandhana and captain Harmanpreet Kaur.

Verma called the milestone long overdue: "It took a lot of years but finally it came, so I'm happy."

Mandhana reached her own landmark earlier in the innings, surpassing New Zealand's Suzie Bates to become the leading run-scorer in women's T20I history during a knock of 37 off 19 balls.

The pair put on a 71-run opening partnership inside the powerplay, setting up India's total of 195-4 in 20 overs at Korogi Athletic Park in Nagoya.

Bangladesh could not keep up the pace, with India bowling them out for just 81 in 15.4 overs.

The result sends India into Tuesday's gold medal final against Sri Lanka. Pakistan will face Bangladesh in the bronze medal match, also on Tuesday.

The Allahabad High Court has directed Uttar Pradesh Police to ensure protection for a Hindu-Muslim same-sex couple whose live-in relationship was being threatened by their family members, local media reported.

In an order dated September 14, Justice Gautam Chowdhary held that the two women are free to live together peacefully without interference from family or anyone else, after personally interacting with the couple and finding both to be adults who had chosen to live together voluntarily, "without pressure, fear or undue influence," according to Bar & Bench, a legal news outlet.

The court directed that if any obstacle arises to their relationship, the police must immediately provide security once they verify both women are of legal age and living together by choice.

The petitioners' counsel told the court the couple faced serious threats to their lives from family members and needed immediate police protection.

The state government opposed the plea, arguing that "there was no acceptance for same-sex relationships" and that such relationships "affect the natural and traditional framework of society," the Times of India reported.

The court rejected that position, holding that living in a relationship is a fundamental right for consenting adult citizens, and that the absence of legal marriage recognition does not entitle anyone to threaten a couple's dignity or physical safety.

The ruling is the latest in a line of similar Allahabad High Court orders protecting same-sex and interfaith couples in Uttar Pradesh, building on earlier decisions, which cited the Supreme Court's 2018 ruling decriminalizing homosexuality in India.

Mumbai police have filed a case against an IIT Bombay professor after a 20-year-old second-year student, Sahil Wakode, was found dead in his hostel room late Thursday, following allegations from his family that he had faced months of caste-based harassment.

Police registered charges against Suryanarayan D. and unidentified others under India's abetment-to-suicide law and provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, local media reported.

Wakode's father, Ravindra Wakode, alleged in his complaint that his son had been subjected to sustained casteist remarks and mental harassment over roughly three months, and that the professor — who was invigilating an exam Wakode was attending on the day he died — used caste-based slurs against him.

The complaint also mentioned the institute's director. Similar complaints were shared by other students, according to The Wire. These allegations have not been independently established.

Meanwhile, IIT Bombay claimed Wakode was found using a mobile phone during the exam, but no disciplinary action was taken. Instead, he had been counseled and assured it would not affect his academic record before he returned to his hostel room.

Students at the scene allege that the professor was seen yelling at Wakode.

IIT Bombay said in a statement shared by local media that "the circumstances surrounding the death are being looked into by the appropriate authorities."

The case has drawn campus protests, with students at IIT Bombay demanding the resignation of both the director and the professor involved. It is reportedly the third student death by suicide at the institute this year, following earlier incidents in February and July.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output.

Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal.

Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average."

"In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India."

He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule.

The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change."

The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

Hello, this is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from around India this weekend.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the inauguration of an international climate conference in New Delhi, saying that developing countries are being unfairly blamed for carbon emissions.

Meanwhile, the Allahabad High Court has directed the Uttar Pradesh Police to ensure the protection of a same-sex couple living together.

Finally, a professor at IIT Bombay is facing allegations of caste abuse after a young student killed himself.

For this and more, follow our blog.

One of the world's most valuable rice varieties, basmati carries strong historic ties to the Punjab region, which spans both India and Pakistan.

Both claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.

But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the fight over basmati rice is far from over.

The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), affiliated with the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), won three of four central posts in this year's Delhi University Students' Union elections, with its candidate Yash Dabas coming in from behind to be elected president.

Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen made history by winning the vice-presidential seat, defeating candidates fielded by both ABVP and the National Students' Union of India (NSUI), the student wing of the Indian National Congress.

In a university facing an acute shortage of hostels, student housing and safety dominated this year's campaign. This came after the September 6 collapse of a paying-guest building in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, which killed seven students.

High rents, non-functional hostels, and a lack of affordable lodging near campus were central issues in candidate platforms.

Declaring his win, Dabas stressed the issue as he addressed the media: "We all witnessed the accident that occurred in Satya Niketan; we do not want such an incident to happen to anyone in the future, and that will be our first priority — conducting safety audits for every college, hostel, and PG."

Shokeen, an NSUI rebel who ran independently, built his campaign partly around the tragedy, vowing not to wear footwear until affected students got justice.

The election also unfolded in the shadow of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led satirical protest movement that organized weeks of demonstrations at Delhi's Jantar Mantar earlier this year, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in national entrance exams.

While the CJP was not involved in the DUSU race directly, the movement shaped how many voters approached the election.

"Students were talking about what or ganisations stand for, whether they agree with their politics and whether voting can give them a greater say in issues concerning students," one student told news agency PTI, adding that many felt they "should not simply vote because a particular organisation has always been influential on campus."

US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients.

The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status.

Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions.

The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful.

The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%.

When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning.

Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia.

He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit."

Surendra Koli, a key figure in India's notorious 2006 Nithari serial killings case who was acquitted of all charges last year, was found dead at a tea stall he operated in Haridwar.

Police are treating the case as a suspected suicide.

Residents discovered Koli's body inside the rented stall and alerted authorities, Haridwar City Deputy Superintendent of Police Shishupal Singh Negi told local media.

No suicide note was found and the body was sent for post-mortem examination as investigators look into the circumstances.

Koli first drew national attention in 2006, when he was a domestic worker at businessman Moninder Singh Pandher's home in Noida. The discovery of human remains, including children's, in a drain behind Pandher's house sparked a major investigation and nationwide outrage.

Koli was convicted and sentenced to death in multiple cases beginning in 2009. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both Koli and Pandher for lack of evidence.

Two key observations were made: Koli's confession was inadmissible, as it was extracted after a long, unauthorized interrogation in police custody without adequate legal safeguards, and the prosecution could not prove that the remains uncovered from the "open, public" drain were based solely on Koli's statements.

The decision was upheld by India's Supreme Court in late 2025.

Reports suggest he moved to the northern city of Haridwar after the acquittal. Police identified Koli through an Aadhaar card found on his body.

A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.

Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.

Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.

"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.

The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."

The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.

Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.

A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.

The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody.

The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail.

Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding.

He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017.

He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued.

Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary.

"Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture."

Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed.

In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon."

The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached.

Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported.

"I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison."

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from and about India this weekend.

We lead our coverage with the news that British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without conviction, has been granted bail.

A UN panel in 2022 recognized it as a case of arbitrary detention, putting the Indian government's human rights record under the microscope.

The Asian Games kick off in Japan on Saturday, but it's not all smooth sailing for the Indian delegation's preparations.

India has announced a last-minute change of its male flagbearer for the opening ceremony after star shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor's ceremonial kit reportedly went missing.

Finally, counting is underway in elections for the Delhi University Student Union, this time under the shadow of the Cockroach Janata Party protests and the collapse of a building in the student hub of Satya Niketan.

For the latest on these stories and more, follow our blog.

card_9.headline: Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
card_9.article_content:
This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of September 19-20, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

We've moved focus to our election special blog covering local races in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Exit polls put the socialist Left Party in first place in Berlin and the far-right Alternative for Germany, AfD, in first place in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Both results mark a defeat for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU party. Merz, who is deeply unpopular, faces a tough road in the weeks to come.

Follow along in our live blog here for the latest updates.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An explosion at a child daycare center has caused part of a building to collapse in the northern German city in Wolfsburg.

The Evangelical Press Service (epd) cited a policewoman as saying that there there were no injuries as there were neither children or staff present.

Residents reported hearing a loud bang around 9 a.m. and called the fire department.

An investigation into the cause of explosion has been launched involving the fire department and the criminal investigation division.

Police do not suspect foul play at this stage.

According to the German Football Association (DFB), investment in women's football by professional clubs has risen by 135% over the past six years. In addition, the number of girls in Germany who play the game has increased by about 30% since 2022.

Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.

Learn more about the growth of women's football in Germany in this report.

The annual German-American Steuben parade took place on Saturday in New York's 5th Avenue.

Dirndls, lederhosen and uniforms along with all manner of hats were on display as participants made their way to the sound of drums and music.

German immigrants make up one of the largest ancestral groups living in the United States.

The Parade was founded in 1957 and named after Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben, a Prussian-born General who served with General George Washington in the American Revolutionary War.

German groups wearing traditional attire, floats, marching bands and dancers, come together from across the US, Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Canada for the parade.

A burglar with an apparent penchant for sweet treats broke into a cafe and opted for cake and ice cream instead of cash, North Rhine-Westphalia police said.

According to investigators, the burglary took place at 2:30 am (0030 GMT) on Saturday in the town of Bad Salzuflen.

"We still do not know whether he deliberately had his sights set on the sweet loot or whether he was seized by a bit of hunger during the crime," a police spokesman said.

Witnesses have been urged to come forward with information they might have that could result in the arrest of the sweet thief.

Germany's automobile giants are continuing to lose ground internationally, according to a new study published on Sunday.

Data compiled by multinational services network EY, previously known as Ernst & Young, found that, while German car manufacturers are still turning over more than their international rivals and still posting a combined profit, the gap is narrowing.

According to the study, German giants BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen turned over a combined €284 billion in the first half of 2026 – around €1.5 billion more than the second-placed Japanese car industry.

But that figure is down 2.9% on last year and 7% lower than the record-high set in 2023.

Profits are also down, with the €13 billion made by the three German market leaders representing the second-lowest half-year profit since 2017.

US, Japanese, Chinese and South Korean manufacturers, on the other hand, all posted record turnovers for the period.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Munich's annual Oktoberfest officially got underway on Saturday when the first beer keg was opened with the traditional cry of O'zapft is! ("It has been tapped!").

But another slogan is also being promoted in Bavaria this year: O'piekst is! ("It has been pricked!") — as doctors offer vaccine jabs against flu and Covid-19.

"With so many people coming together in such tight spaces in the beer tents, the risk of infection at Oktoberfest is higher," explained Christoph Spinner, head of infectiology at Munich's Rechts der Isar hospital.

Oktoberfest coincides with the start of the annual flu season, and Spinner warned that less than a third of people who are recommended a flu jab have actually had one.

Beatrix Zurek, a health expert from the city-led initiative München impft! ("Munich vaccinates!") said: "It's our job to go where people are. And that means: Oktoberfest."

Guten Morgen! And welcome back to our coverage of Germany on Sunday, 20 September.

Voters in two more German states head to the polls today as elections take place in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and in the capital, the city-state of Berlin.

We will have all you need to know about those elections in a separate blog which we will be launching when polls open at 8 a.m. local time, so keep an eye out for that.

And for all your non-election Germany news – stay right here!

We are pausing our coverage on Saturday, 19 September and will be back on Sunday, 20 September with more headlines from Germany.

Protests against abortion and assisted suicide took to the streets of the German capital Berlin as well as the western city of Cologne on Saturday, in protest dubbed "March for Life."

Police said some 2,200 took part in Berlin, whereas no figures on the Cologne protests were immediately available. Catholic bishops were among those attending.

Meanwhile in both cities, pro-choice protests were also held.

Abortion in Germany is banned but women are allowed to carry out the measure if the first 12 weeks of the pregnancy have not yet concluded. They are however obligated to hold consultations first, and the abortion can only be held at least three days after such consultations.

Exceptions are naturally if the pregnancy poses a risk to the woman's health.

Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and one of Germany’s most prominent Jewish community leaders, has voiced her alarm at the Alternative for Germany's (AfD) landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.

Speaking to DW, she warned that some Jews are once again considering leaving Germany, saying years of efforts to rebuild trust after the Holocaust are being undermined. Knobloch described the rise of the far-right party as a serious threat, urged mainstream politicians to confront extremism more forcefully and called for greater engagement with young people.

Her comments come amid renewed concerns about antisemitism, political polarization, and reported death threats against her.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party held on Saturday its final rally in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the Sunday vote in the eastern state.

Ulrich Siegmund, the party's winner in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, addressed a rally of some 1,000 AfD supporters in Schwerin, according to police estimates.

He said that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won but without an absolute majority, was also possible in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The latest ZDF Politbarometer poll puts the AfD in the eastern state one percentage point behind the Social Democrats (SPD); at 36% and 37% respectively. Next is the Left Party (Die Linke) at 9%, then the CDU at 6% and the Greens at 5%.

The AfD rally was also attended by the party's candidate in the state, Leif-Erik Holm, who echoed previous remarks that the election "should serve as a signal that this government must finally go." Several other AfD leaders have repeated the same calls since the results of the Saxony-Anhalt state vote.

The far-right party's final rally of the campaign also saw some 350 counter-demonstrators, according to police. No incidents were reported.

In an unusual measure, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will convene the Christian Democratic Union leadership on Sunday to discuss the results of the state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

Unlike in previous state elections, Merz has invited the entire party executive committee to a formal meeting at 5:00 p.m. (1500 GMT) at the CDU headquarters in Berlin. The committee includes some 25 members, either electees or representatives by virtue of their offices.

Due to attend are the eight influential CDU premiers who backed him ahead of the election.

Compounding pressure has befallen the conservative chancellor since the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month, which saw the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narrowly missing out on an absolute majority, while Merz's CDU secured half their previous result.

Polls for the upcoming votes are also grim, with the CDU threatened with the prospect of falling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.

In the capital Berlin, where CDU is currently in power, polls suggest the conservative party is in a neck-and-neck race with the socialist Left Party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's highest ranking military officer, General Carsten Breuer, will be the next chairman of NATO's Military Committee, after being voted into the role on Saturday.

"The support of the chiefs of defense of our NATO allies means a great deal to me. The alliance faces major challenges - for our security and peace in Europe and beyond," Breuer, who is also Germany's chief of defense, told German news agency DPA.

The position is considered among NATO's most influential ones.

Breuer succeeds Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and will take over as of July 2027.

Breuer was competing for the position against Canada's Chief of Defense General Jennie Carignan. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to head the committee.

Cologne's cultural complex, which includes the city's main opera house, theater and children's opera, has finally reopened after renovation works that extended for some 14 years.

"With the reopening of our theaters, we are giving the city back a central place of meeting, inspiration and artistic freedom that belongs to all people of Cologne," Mayor Torsten Burmester said.

The western German state's opera house dates back to 1957, with the theater coming shortly after in 1962.

Since 2012, renovations on the pair commenced with an original budget of €250 million (roughly $287 million) that has somehow multiplied nearly three fold as the years rolled on.

The final price tag on the refurbishments stood at around €800 million.

In the 14 years it took to get the job done, Cologne's opera and theater houses had to relocate to other venues.

Celebrations of the reopening include music, dance, as well as other hands-on activities. On Sunday evening, the opening ceremony will conclude with a concert at the opera house.

card_1.headline: 'Agent Layla': Sex assault victim turned secret agent brings her abuser to justice
card_1.article_content:
WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

On a Friday morning in 2021, just a couple of days before Halloween, Vienna Luke zipped up an oversized puffer jacket with a big hood, and put on sunglasses to hide her face.

In a SUV outside her home, plainclothes RCMP officers waited to whisk her away on a secret mission — a face-to-face meeting with the man responsible for the worst night of her life.

Luke, a fitness instructor and mother of two children, was the key undercover agent in an RCMP operation that — if successful — could lead to the rarest of outcomes: a criminal conviction in a sexual assault that had occurred 14 years earlier.

If Luke failed, her case and the truth about what had happened that night would almost surely be lost to time.

The police referred to Luke using a code name: Agent Layla.

'The whole thing really was conditional on me,' said Vienna Luke. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

CBC has obtained the surreptitious recording of that mission. It shows an extremely rare instance of RCMP turning the victim into an agent in her own case.

The RCMP sergeant who led the investigation says it’s an approach that is almost never tried  — especially in sexual assault cases.

"For the victim to have the strength, and the investigative team [to have the] determination[...] is almost unheard of," said Sgt. Joëlle LaChance.

Facing the man who assaulted her, her estranged brother-in-law, "Agent Layla" presses him for answers over the course of 70 minutes. Luke ultimately elicits a confession that surpassed even the highest hopes of the RCMP team gathered in a nearby hotel room listening in over a wire. The breakthrough was so moving that it brought tears to a hardened undercover officer accustomed to working with drug dealers and murderers.

"She literally took her life back in her hands," said one of the officers from the undercover unit, working with LaChance.

"There wasn’t a dry eye in that room," said LaChance.

Police hid a microphone in a purse Vienna Luke carried into a meeting with the man who assaulted her. The police set up for the face-to-face meeting in a hotel room above a Vancouver International Airport lounge. (Shawnessy Luke)

That recording — along with interviews from Luke, her middle sister Shawnessy Luke, and the police officers involved in the sting — is part of a new four-part CBC podcast called Personally: Agent Layla.

The podcast details how Luke managed to get the truth, put the man who assaulted her behind bars, and begin to heal from an incident that left her traumatized, detached from her own body, and at odds with members of her family who at times failed to take her side.

(Chloe Cushman)

At 20 years old, Luke was living at home with her family in the Vancouver suburbs after attending a Bible school overseas. Her life had been sheltered; she says she had never been kissed, or even held hands with a man.

While she contemplated her future, she decided to move in with her eldest sister, brother-in-law and their sons in the small B.C. town of Fort St. John — a 14-hour drive north from where she was raised.

Fort St. John, B.C., with a population of about 21,000 people, is a 14-hour drive north from the Vancouver suburb where Vienna Luke was raised. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

Her brother-in-law, Justin Sewell, was a respected veterinarian who was active in a local Christian church. Sewell was 11 years older than her and he had been a trusted member of the family since Luke was a child.

During a week when Luke's sister and nephews were out of town, Sewell proposed a plan. He suggested she get drunk for the first time at home with him, in what he described as a "safe place."

Luke says she had heard of another Christian girl who had done something similar to experiment for the first time with drinking, so she went along with his idea.

WARNING: This story contains graphic details about sexual abuse.

According to testimony presented in court and extensive interviews conducted by the CBC, Luke only sipped the cocktails he made — one of them a Kahlua-based "Brown Cow."

As she and Sewell danced to country music in the living room, Luke remembers her legs buckling. As the world went black, she felt nauseous and thought to herself that drinking alcohol didn’t seem so fun after all.

Aloud, she spoke a phrase that only drives home how naive she was to what was about to happen.

"I just love Jesus," she said. "I just love Jesus. And then I was out."

For Luke, everything about the rest of that night is blank, except for one memory that would both torment her and propel her to seek accountability in the almost two decades to come: a brief moment when she says she awoke mostly naked in her bed.

"I was looking at myself, from above, to my brother-in-law taking off my underwear," she said.

In the aftermath of that horrible evening, Luke says she tried to "shelve" what happened. For months, she fought what she described as a war between her body that remembered, and her brain trying to forget.

She moved back home to her parents’ home near Vancouver and didn’t come face-to-face with Sewell again until half-a-year later at Christmas when the entire family went to Florida for a cruise. But when they said their goodbyes at the airport, her middle sister, Shawnessy Luke, noticed something was off.

"I remember it like it was yesterday," Shawnessy Luke said. "The way he hugged her. And I think that’s strange. That’s prolonged. And I knew something was going on."

Shawnessy Luke believed her sister, Vienna, when she began to open up. (Allison Luke)

Shawnessy Luke describes herself as a person with great intuition and "like a dog with a bone." She waited until she and Vienna Luke got back to their parents' home to ask questions. She was doing her laundry in the family’s narrow utility room when she insisted that her sister explain.

"She definitely pulled it out of me," said Vienna Luke. "I did not volunteer."

Vienna Luke told her sister what happened in the days leading up to the drinking game, facts that were accepted in court: How Sewell had held her hand, how he called her up from her basement bedroom to watch a lightning storm and then massaged her back, and how he told her he loved her.

Then she shared how Sewell proposed she get drunk, and how she couldn’t remember much more than that.

"In my moral compass brain, the minute I heard those things, I was like, I don’t need to know anymore, I believe you," said Shawnessy Luke. "We’ve got to tell someone about this because [...] whatever happened to you [...] was wrong."

Shawnessy Luke says she insisted they tell their mom and dad.

Middle sister Shawnessy Luke has stuck by her sister's side through all the steps of the investigation. 'I'm here in support of her going through this process. That's my goal. That's the only reason I'm here.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The night in question had happened in June 2007, about 10 years before the #MeToo social movement. As Vienna Luke told her parents about Sewell holding her hand and massaging her back, she stopped short of sharing the most damning memory of all — that she woke up to Sewell removing her underwear. She felt like her parents didn’t know how to handle what she was saying, and didn't have the vocabulary at the time to talk about sexual assault.

"I knew that I couldn’t share more," she said.

Her father called Sewell right away. She didn’t overhear their conversation, but she recalls her father handed her the phone and she found herself suddenly on the line with Sewell.

Vienna Luke pleaded with Sewell to tell his wife what had happened, hoping her oldest sister would take her side. She still doesn’t know if that happened, only that her oldest sister has continued to stand by her husband and is still married to him today.

Her parents declined to be interviewed for this story. In a victim impact statement filed in court, they wrote: "Our effort to uncover the full story was unsuccessful. Lacking information and clarity, we had no path forward. We felt uneasy about what we knew, but did not pursue this matter further."

In the years that followed, the Luke family struggled with the divide created by that night: Vienna’s oldest sister and Sewell on one side, Shawnessy and Vienna Luke on the other, and their parents trying to walk a line between all three of their daughters.

"It was easier to take Justin for his word," Vienna Luke said. "He was the one that knew what happened. He got to write the story."

Vienna Luke in 2014, seven years after the horrible night. 'I was just a robot,' she said. 'I was going through the motions of what I thought I was supposed to be doing.' (Allison White)

With no clarity about what had actually happened and that one horrific memory of him removing her underwear replaying in her head, Luke says she spent years feeling like a robot trying to numb her pain.

She also moved out of her parents' house and moved to Vancouver, got a job, and met a man who she credits for showing her how to love herself again.

When they started a family, Luke says something inside her started to shift. She knew she’d have to tell her children the truth someday, and something about birth reconnected her to her body.

"My body wasn’t just laboring," she wrote in her journal. "[It was] waking up."

Twelve years after the assault, and weeks after she delivered her second child, Luke called up her sister Shawnessy.

"Hey, I’m ready to deal with this," she said.

So the two sisters made a list.

Together, they wrote down all the names of people they suspected had soured on Sewell after he had disclosed to his wife and friends two extramarital affairs five years earlier.

Shawnessy Luke's first call was to one of those ex-lovers, a female veterinarian who had worked at Sewell's clinic.

Justin Sewell's veterinarian clinic in Fort St. John, B.C. (Matt Prepost)

In a recording of that phone call shared with CBC and in court testimony, the woman said she and Sewell were discussing previous sexual experiences when he said something shocking.

"So what he told me was that he put ketamine in [Vienna’s] drinks," the ex-lover revealed during a phone call Shawnessy Luke recorded. "But he didn’t know how much was enough to like, make her forget."

The sisters say this new information validated a hunch they had come to believe: that Vienna Luke had been drugged.

It also gave her a little piece of evidence to march into the Vancouver Police Department and report.

Vienna Luke's file was transferred up to the small RCMP detachment in Fort St. John. Against all odds, it landed on the desk of Sgt. Joëlle LaChance, a female officer with a special commitment to cases that many officers would simply dismiss as too hard and too old.

"My whole life I have been a champion for the underdog," she said. "Being able to stand up for the victim … it's why I do my job."

'Being able to stand up for the victim — it's why I do my job,' said RCMP Sgt. Joëlle LaChance. (submitted by Joëlle LaChance)

LaChance said she knew Sewell — with his stellar reputation in the community, had a lot to lose. So instead of going directly to the veterinarian to question him, she called on other RCMP units for help, including the undercover unit.

Together, they hatched a plan.

Court records show Sewell had emailed Vienna Luke several times in the years since the night of the drinking game, asking her to accept that he had changed and hoping that the extended family could be together again.

Luke showed the police those emails. Together, they crafted back emails that suggested there could be a possibility for family reconciliation, but first Luke would need the whole truth and they’d have to meet face-to-face.

They pitched Sewell on a plan to fly to Vancouver to meet Luke.

Unbeknownst to Sewell, Luke would be prepared.

Vienna Luke carried this piece of paper with her into the undercover operation at YVR airport. Her notes came from training with the RCMP. (Vienna Luke)

For weeks, she trained, preparing to grill him for the facts. She spent a couple of days in a hotel room, sitting across from an undercover RCMP officer who role played with her. The officer worked to get her comfortable asking tough, direct questions, using words like "vagina" and "ejaculate" — specific terms that would be necessary for charges to be laid.

"This isn’t a trained hitman," the undercover officer said. "She’s very polite, very soft-spoken. And I knew that was exactly the opposite of what we were going to need to do."

Something changed for Vienna Luke when she became a mother. 'My firstborn, [...] my constant reminder that I am lovable,' she wrote in her journal. 'My second child, [...] you showed me a bravery I didn't know I had.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

On the day of the sting at Vancouver airport, everyone involved held their breath. RCMP had laid the groundwork, but as soon as the tape started recording and Sewell walked in, it would be entirely up to Luke to get the truth.

For the plan to work, Luke would need to be both victim and hero. The RCMP believed it was the best chance at bringing charges. Luke knew it was her only chance to get answers.

"You think I'm exactly the same," Luke remembered thinking. "You think I'm gonna play your same little game, but we've got a new game and I'm writing it."

In the recording, Sewell sits down across from Luke and quickly tries to take control. He claims pornography and a culture that objectifies women is part of why he assaulted her that night.

"Okay, but you’re not actually telling me what happened," Luke replies. "Let’s get back to the night and what actually … happened."

The undercover officer who had spent time coaching Luke for this moment felt proud.

"Take control of that conversation," he said in an interview while listening back to the recording. "Don’t just accept a two-minute fluffy bullshit answer."

An excerpt from the transcript submitted in court of the surreptitious recording between Vienna Luke (VL) and Justin Sewell (JS). (CBC)

Luke persists, peppering Sewell with questions seeking specific details, seemingly undeterred by the fact she’s learning this information about the worst night of her life for the first time.

On tape, Sewell confesses to drugging her, removing her clothing, masturbating and ejaculating twice on her body, and taking 30 photos, including ones where he is spooning her naked body and one where his penis is near her face.

As Luke prepares to wrap up, she lobs an open ended question.

"Is there anything that I’m not asking?" Luke said.

"No reason for me to disclose this. But I took pictures of you at other times," Sewell replied.

His response allowed the RCMP to recommend another charge, this one for voyeurism.

On the morning of April 26, 2022, Fort St. John RCMP arrested Sewell as he left his home for work.

LaChance said this case was a big deal for the small Fort St. John RCMP detachment. 'People didn't believe we could do it,' she said. 'I believed with Vienna as the agent that we could do it because she was showing the strength and wanting to have justice.' (Tom Summer/CBC)

Sewell pleaded guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism — one for the photos he took of her the night he assaulted her and one for times he had watched her through her bedroom window. Crown agreed to stay a charge of administering a drug with intent to commit a sexual assault.

In the courtroom, Luke’s mother, father, and Sewell’s supporters listened to the recording from the airport.

A provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to house arrest. Crown appealed and the Court of Appeal judges determined the lower court judge had overstated the mitigating fact of Sewell’s confession.

They issued a sentence of 33 months less a day in prison for his crimes.

Luke asked the court to remove the publication ban on her name — something that is standard in cases of sexual assault to protect the victim’s identity.

As she began to tell friends and acquaintances her whole story, that she was the unnamed victim, she says she realized how important it was to her that she could also say she was the secret agent.

Vienna Luke is telling her story for the first time publicly in a new CBC Podcast called Agent Layla. (Vienna Luke)

"It took this … experiment of the police saying, 'Hey, how about you go undercover as yourself' for me to realize, whoa, look at the advocate I can be for myself," she said.

"I was Agent Layla. That's me."

The CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla is available wherever you get your podcasts.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

card_2.headline: Head of European Investment Bank eyes Canada opportunities as Carney pushes EU ties
card_2.article_content:
The president of the European Union's investment bank says "the time is ripe" to deepen its co-operation with Canada by exploring how to finance Canadian projects — comments that come as Prime Minister Mark Carney pushes for more EU ties.

"We haven't been very active in Canada until now," said Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank (EIB) in an exclusive interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday morning.

But Calviño, who is visiting Canada to meet with various federal ministers, said her trip "clearly shows that in Europe, we put our money where our mouth is."

card_3.headline: La Bola Negra headlines TIFF Awards with People's Choice nod
card_3.article_content:
La Bola Negra has won the People's Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival.

The film, directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, is an epic that spans the interconnected lives of three gay men in Spain. TIFF announced its suite of festival awards on Sunday.

Other big winners include Angh, which nabbed the Platform Award, a jury prize that comes with a $20,000 purse.

The film from director Theja Rio is about the last surviving chief of a Nagaland village on the Indo-Burma border.

For the first time this year, the Platform Award offers a direct route to the best international feature film category at the Academy Awards.

The Academy previously only accepted one submission from each country for that category, but this year it expanded its criteria to consider winners of qualifying awards at international film festivals.

The Platform Award is one of six such prizes, but other eligibility criteria still apply, including that at least half of the film must be in a language other than English.

Because Angh is mostly in Konyak, it qualifies for best international feature contention.

Best Canadian Discovery for a first- or second-time director went to Cody Lightning for his sophomore feature Smudge the Blades.

"I come to you today with a heavy heart and beer on my breath," Lightning said as he accepted the award, saying his mother — also a filmmaker — died several weeks ago.

"I get my humour from my dad, I get my storytelling from my mom," he said through tears. "This one's for my mom. This one's for my mom. This one's for my mom."

Best Canadian Feature went to Sunburn by Serville Poblete, a coming-of-age film about a group of kids from Toronto's Bleecker Street.

The FIPRESCI Prize, which goes to a first-time international filmmaker, was awarded to Ancestors by Irish writer-director David Turpin, about an Irishman in London in the 1980s, when homosexuality was still illegal in Ireland.

The NETPAC Award, which recognizes movies from Asia and the Pacific, went to the Palestinian film Thirteen in Gaza by Hosam Abu Dan, about a 13-year-old girl living in a refugee camp in the Gaza Strip.

card_4.headline: Germany's Merz vows to press on with reforms despite state election losses to far-right AfD
card_4.article_content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered a bruising electoral setback in two state elections on Sunday, including a historic defeat for his party, but vowed to press ahead with potentially painful reforms to Europe's biggest economy.

Exit polls by public broadcaster ARD on Sunday night indicated that Merz's centre-right Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, came in with just five per cent in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the lowest result ever since the Second World War for the party in any state. The anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party made significant gains Sunday.

Merz acknowledged his party's result as a "disaster" but struck a defiant note, rejecting any retreat from his government's reform agenda. He argued that Germany's economic and political problems made difficult and potentially unpopular reforms more urgent, not less, and pledged to press ahead.

"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said in a statement shortly after the exit polls were announced on public television. "I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."

In Berlin, the CDU was projected to come in second with 20 per cent, behind the Left party at 24.5 per cent, according to ARD's exit poll.

AfD win seen as big victory for far right politics in Germany

Merz's authority was already damaged by CDU's stinging defeat to AfD in the Sept. 6 election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. That result shocked many Germans who had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution.

Merz, 70, became Germany's leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years, but he has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has himself become deeply unpopular.

Far-right victory in German state expected to send shockwaves throughout the world

The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election, where it has best chance yet of forming the country's first far-right regional government since the Second World War, has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well. In the past two weeks, there have been calls even from within his own party to replace him as chancellor, although no top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against "personnel debates."

Apparently anticipating a tough post-election period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the UN General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he's determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.

card_5.headline: Paredes' 62-yard field goal lifts Stampeders to 40-38 win over winless Redblacks
card_5.article_content:
A 62-yard field goal by Rene Paredes, for the longest of his career, with two seconds remaining gave the Calgary Stampeders a 40-38 win over the visiting Ottawa Redblacks in the CFL on Saturday.

Quincy Vaughn scored a pair of short-yardage rushing touchdowns and Tevin Jones and Jalen Philpot each caught touchdown passes for Calgary (6-8), which stayed in the playoff conversation, albeit in last place in the West Division.

Paredes also produced field goals from 57, 23 and 19 yards, as well as four convert points in front of an announced 20,113 at McMahon Stadium.

Quarterback McLeod Bethel-Thompson, in his first start for Ottawa this season, threw five touchdown passes and Keelan White caught three of them as the Redblacks fell to 0-13 on the season.

The Redblacks became just the second team in CFL history to start a season with 13 straight losses after the Shreveport Pirates in 1994.

They've now lost 19 consecutive games, dating back to last season.

'Nowhere else to go but up': Redblacks superfan stays positive amid historic losing streak

This team had the CFL record for longest losing streak for 33 years - before the Redblacks snatched it up

Justin Hardy's touchdown catch with 72 seconds remaining and Brett Lauther's convert point gave the Redblacks at 38-37 lead.

Kalil Pimpleton caught a touchdown pass in the third quarter to cut Calgary's lead to a field goal heading into the fourth quarter.

Lauther missed a field-goal attempt from 43 yards, but was good from 37 yards and added four convert points.

Bethel-Thompson, 38, completed 27 of 48 pass attempts for 379 yards and was intercepted once.

Ottawa Redblacks' Justin Hardy, front, dives for a pass against the Calgary Stampeders during first half CFL football action in Calgary, Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Calgary quarterback Vernon Adams Jr. was 28-for-41 in passing for 357 yards and two touchdowns. He was intercepted for a fifth time in five games after a clean sheet in his first eight games this season.

Adams went down clutching his left ankle after contact with one of his offensive lineman early in the third quarter.

He returned to play the next series, however, and orchestrated a seven-play, 57-yard touchdown drive finished by Vaughn for Calgary's 24-14 lead.

But Bethel-Thompson connected with Pimpleton on a 28-yard catch and run to score. Lauther and Paredes traded field goals early in the fourth quarter.

Bethel-Thompson threw to White at Calgary's nine-yard line and the 24-year-old from North Vancouver, B.C., ran the ball in for a four-point lead.

But the Stampeders countered with a 63-yard march that concluded with Philpot's 26-yard catch in the end zone to re-take the lead 34-31.

Zy Alexander picked off a Bethel-Thompson throw on the Redblack's subsequent drive that bounced out of Hardy's hands to give Calgary the ball on Ottawa's 23-yard line.

The Stampeders managed only a field goal to lead by six points with just over two minutes to play.

Their defence thought Ottawa turned the ball over on downs on the Redblacks' next drive, but Ottawa kept the drive alive on a successful pass interference challenge by coach Ryan Dinwiddie.

Bethel-Thompson threw 15 yards to Hardy for a one-point lead. The game was left to the leg of Paredes after Calgary's offence struggled to push deep into Ottawa territory.

Calgary was up 17-14 at halftime after Adams aired the ball downfield to Jones for a 60-yard touchdown with 36 seconds remaining.

Ottawa Redblacks' Kyahva Tezino, top left, chases Calgary Stampeders quarterback Vernon Adams Jr. during second half CFL football action in Calgary, Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Ottawa led for the first time in the game with a minute left in the first half. Bethel-Thompson found White in the end zone a second time in a three-minute span with a 25-yard throw for a 14-10 lead.

Calgary's Paredes drilled a low, hard kick 57 yards with the wind behind him for a field goal.

Stampeders looking to start season strong ahead of Calgary hosting Grey Cup

After failing to cash a second-quarter interception of Adams into points and then turning the ball over on downs on Calgary's 11-yard line, Ottawa scored just inside the three-minute warning when Bethel-Thompson threw 19 yards to White in the end zone

Temperature at kickoff was 22 C, with winds gusting to 44 km/h.

The Redblacks host the Stampeders next Saturday in the second game of a home and home.
