card_7.headline: Kindergartener dropped off at wrong bus stop, found wandering through apartment building
card_7.author: Jenna Legge
card_7.article_content:
An Ottawa-and-area school board says it's taking steps to avoid a repeat of a recent incident in which a kindergarten student was dropped off after school at the wrong place and was found wandering the halls of an apartment building.

At around 2:30 p.m. on Aug. 26, Em McLellan said she heard screaming coming from the hallway in her apartment building.

Being an educational assistant and mom of four, she said she could tell right away that something was wrong.

"I knew that shriek from a child ... wasn't fun, it was grave," she said.

McLellan opened her door to find a boy who she described as around three or four years old and "inconsolable, crying out for his mom."

Along with another woman in the apartment complex, McLellan tried to speak with the child. However, she said he only spoke French and her attempts were unsuccessful.

After going through the child's bookbag, McLellan said she found out the boy is a student at Laurier-Carrière Catholic Elementary School, which is about a six-minute drive from her apartment. She called the school but again had trouble communicating.

"I couldn't understand the English and they couldn't understand my French, and it was just, it was a disaster," she said. "I was just furious. I was beyond furious."

It was then that McLellan called police, who she said arrived within about 10 minutes.

"This child was put in a situation [where] anybody could have taken them," she said.

An apartment building in the complex in Nepean where a kindergartener was found after they were dropped off at the wrong bus stop in Ottawa. (Gabrielle Huston/CBC)

The Ottawa Police Service confirmed it received a call just after 3 p.m. that day from someone reporting they had found a child, adding that officers reunited the young pupil with his family.

Police said the parent told officers the school bus had mistakenly dropped the child off at the wrong location.

CBC News connected with parents at the school to try and speak with the family of the boy, but did not hear back by the time of publication.

The school board and police did not share the family's contact details due to privacy concerns.

In a French-language emailed statement to CBC News, the Conseil des écoles catholiques du Centre-Est (CECCE) confirmed the incident took place, stating that the student got off the bus at the stop before their assigned stop.

The school board said more than 25 students got off at the bus stop where the child was dropped off and that several parents were present at the drop-off, but that the standard verification procedure was not properly followed during disembarkation.

CECCE added that the kindergartener’s parents contacted the school when they realized their child did not arrive at the correct stop.

The board also said it has various measures in place to ensure the safety of students being transported, including the use of colour-coded tags to identify students and direct them to their assigned bus.

The board said it's concerned about the incident and is taking steps to avoid another like it, including following up with the Le Consortium de transport scolaire d'Ottawa (CTSO) and the transportation service provider to ensure that existing safety procedures are strictly followed and that such a situation does not happen again.

Patrick Pharand, director of the CTSO, echoed the board’s statements in an email to CBC News, saying they too are following up with the transportation provider.

According to the CTSO rules on its website, kindergarten students require a parent or designated person to be present when that child is getting off the bus.

CBC News followed up with CTSO to ask if the bus driver will face any consequences but did not hear back by publication.

card_8.headline: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like in much of the country, it's not so simple

card_8.article_content:
To an outsider, the 3.2-hectare sea of grass surrounding the Elgin County Railway Museum in the heart of St. Thomas, Ont., might look like an urban park. That's not what Wil Zufelt sees.

To him, it's an enormous open wound.

"You say green space," he said. "We're actually sitting in the middle of a brownfield site that was left behind from the railroads."

Built in 1913, the hulking red-brick building was once the Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops, where locomotives were maintained and overhauled by a staff of 400 workers. It's one of three survivors of a sprawling railway complex that once had 112 buildings.

The old building is now a museum, but it can't welcome visitors. It's literally crumbling. The city engineer ordered it closed after finding its walls were bowing and its ceiling was unsafe.

"People need to wake up," Zufelt said. "Pay attention to what we're losing."

Zufelt heads Railworks, the organization behind three of St. Thomas's surviving railway landmarks. He's launching a campaign to raise $8 million to save and restore the former locomotive shops.

The goal is to turn the old locomotive shops into not just a museum, but an active gathering place at the centre of a redeveloped downtown.

"I want it to be more than alive. I want it to be the centre of St. Thomas," he said. "That's what success is, is putting a heartbeat back in the core and then you have your arteries and everything pumps out from the middle."

By 1914, eight railways converged on St. Thomas, bringing more than 100 trains through the southwestern Ontario city every day. Its location made it a major hub for American rail traffic between Detroit and Buffalo and between New York and Chicago. The cross-border connection was so important, at one point, St. Thomas even had a U.S. consulate.

Today, the community that calls itself the "Railway City" has no rail connection at all.

The railways are long gone, but their remains are scattered across the city — empty lots filled with rubble from where railway buildings once stood, abandoned shunting yards, railway spikes that turn up like seashells on a beach and tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere.

The old London to Port Stanley Railway runs past a restored station in St. Thomas before it abruptly ends — disappearing into the grass of a residential neighbourhood.

The missing connection was the subject of a 1990 federal transport order requiring CN to replace the missing diamond at its own expense once the line reached CN tracks. But the physical connection was never completed.

Today, part of the former route is blocked by a parking lot enclosed by a fence.

The Canadian Transport Agency told CBC News the order remains in effect and CN's obligation would still apply if the physical connection were made.

CN did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

St. Thomas is an unusually stark example of what happened in communities across Canada as the railway era receded, according to Thomas Blampied, a historian who studied Canada's railway history at the University of Toronto.

The former Canada Southern Railway Station in St. Thomas, Ont., is one of the surviving landmarks from an era when the city was one of Canada's busiest railway centres. The 1873 building is one of three remaining historic railway buildings in a community that once had 112. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"Cars started to eat away at passenger revenue from railways and trucks started to take some of the freight traffic," he said.

As passengers moved to cars and freight moved to trucks, railways abandoned increasingly unprofitable routes. They didn't simply stop running trains. Much of the infrastructure was removed with them.

"Do we keep the infrastructure — so the track, all the signals, all the crossing warnings — do we keep it all intact?" Blampied said. "Increasingly, the answer was no."

In some cases, the rails were sold for scrap, in many cases, he said, "it made economic sense to completely withdraw."

But even where the railway lines survived, the network changed.

Anthony Perl, a transportation policy expert at Simon Fraser University, said railways removed passing tracks and other infrastructure once passenger trains disappeared, reshaping the network around the needs of freight.

The Northern Ontario tourism sector are hoping the return of the Northlander passenger train will help bring more people to the region. (Submitted by Ontario Northland)

"We had a great streamlining, or right-sizing, or value engineering, pick your term — of the national rail infrastructure in Canada as passenger trains went away," Perl said. "To optimize it for long, slow freight trains."

He said that matters now because Canada is trying to put passenger trains back on a network that, in many places, was either removed or rebuilt for another purpose.

In Ontario, the province is preparing to restore Northlander passenger service between Toronto and northeastern Ontario, more than a decade after it was cancelled. The federal government meanwhile, is developing Alto, a new high-speed passenger railway between Toronto and Quebec City that would run largely on its own tracks.

Other communities are pushing for passenger rail to return, including on Vancouver Island, in Alberta between Calgary and Banff and in Cape Breton.

But Canada's railways have something airlines and trucking companies don't: control over the infrastructure they use.

Abandoned freight cars sit on overgrown tracks in a former shunting yard in St. Thomas, Ont., one of the remnants of the city's once sprawling railway network that linked major North American cities. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"No one is going to build an alternative set of rails across this country under any circumstances," Perl said. "That's why they make the call on whether to put in or take out tracks in particular places."

In St. Thomas, CN has yet to restore the missing connection between London and Port Stanley.

"Even when the Canadian Transportation Agency orders them to do something they don't want to do," he said, "it can take quite a while, if ever, that they will go along with it because they have the ownership of that infrastructure."

Perl argues that kind of power has deep roots in the railway business and points to language the industry has given us.

"To 'railroad someone' is to take advantage and treat someone unfairly or unjustly," he said. "You don't see that with too many other industries."

The Academy previously only accepted one submission from each country for that category, but this year it expanded its criteria to consider winners of qualifying awards at international film festivals.

The Platform Award is one of six such prizes, but other eligibility criteria still apply, including that at least half of the film must be in a language other than English.

Because Angh is mostly in Konyak, it qualifies for best international feature contention.

Best Canadian Discovery for a first- or second-time director went to Cody Lightning for his sophomore feature Smudge the Blades.

"I come to you today with a heavy heart and beer on my breath," Lightning said as he accepted the award, saying his mother — also a filmmaker — died several weeks ago.

"I get my humour from my dad, I get my storytelling from my mom," he said through tears. "This one's for my mom. This one's for my mom. This one's for my mom."

Best Canadian Feature went to Sunburn by Serville Poblete, a coming-of-age film about a group of kids from Toronto's Bleecker Street.

Rounding out the other People's Choice winners are Elsinore by Simon Stone for international People's Choice; Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney for Midnight Madness; and Barry Avrich's Darlene Love: I Know Where I've Been for People’s Choice documentary.

This is the second-straight year Avrich has won that prize. Last year he was the surprise winner for The Road Between Us, a documentary about an Israeli general's rescue mission on Oct. 7, 2023.

The FIPRESCI Prize, which goes to a first-time international filmmaker, was awarded to Ancestors by Irish writer-director David Turpin, about an Irishman in London in the 1980s, when homosexuality was still illegal in Ireland.

The NETPAC Award, which recognizes movies from Asia and the Pacific, went to the Palestinian film Thirteen in Gaza by Hosam Abu Dan, about a 13-year-old girl living in a refugee camp in the Gaza Strip.
